title: Washing Feet
lead: In the Bible's world, washing a guest's feet was a basic act of hospitality, usually done by a slave. Abraham offers water for his visitors' feet, Abigail offers to wash the feet of David's servants, a sinful woman washes Jesus's feet with her tears, and at the last supper Jesus washes his disciples' feet and tells them to do the same. Some churches keep foot washing as an ordinance; others see it as an example of humble service.

sections.b: People walked dusty roads in sandals, so a host offered water to wash the feet (Genesis 18:4; 19:2; 24:32; Judges 19:21). Washing someone else's feet was a servant's task and a sign of deep humility (1 Samuel 25:41). Jesus rebukes Simon the Pharisee for giving him no water for his feet (Luke 7:44), and 1 Timothy 5:10 lists washing the saints' feet among the good works of a faithful widow.
sections.refs: Genesis 18:4; Genesis 19:2; Genesis 24:32; Judges 19:21; 1 Samuel 25:41; Luke 7:44; 1 Timothy 5:10

sections.b: By the 300s some churches washed the feet of the newly baptized; Ambrose of Milan did, and noted that Rome did not. The washing became part of the Holy Thursday liturgy in the Catholic and Orthodox churches. Anabaptists (Dordrecht Confession, 1632), Brethren, Seventh-day Adventists, Free Will Baptists and the Church of God (Cleveland) keep it as an ordinance, often with the Lord's Supper. Reformed and most Baptist churches treat John 13:14 as an example of service rather than a command to repeat the act.
